1.title: Requirements, Research, Planning and Process Optimization
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Requirements, Research, Planning and Process Optimization. This module covers requirements, research, planning and process optimization. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. How to use Claude to analyze requirements and clarify a request before work starts. How to identify good use cases for Claude and screen out poor ones. How to use Claude for research and planning. How to improve a process step by step and measure the result.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Returns Overhaul
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Returns Overhaul. Customer care says: "Returns take too long and customers complain.". The project manager asks Claude to turn the complaint into requirements: who is affected, what "too long" means, what must not change, and what success looks like. The result is a short requirements list and eight open questions to take to stakeholders.

1.title: Analyzing Requirements
1.text: Analyzing Requirements. Claude can help you move from a vague wish to a clear, testable requirement.

1.title: Analyzing Requirements, continued
1.text: Analyzing Requirements, continued. Clarify the goal. "Restate this request in one sentence and list what is unclear". List stakeholders and needs. "Who is affected by a returns change? What does each need?". Turn notes into requirements. "From these interview notes, list functional needs, constraints and assumptions". Write user stories and acceptance criteria. "Write stories in the form 'As a..., I want..., so that...' with pass or fail criteria". Find gaps and conflicts. "Which requirements conflict or are ambiguous?". Prepare questions. "List the questions I should ask the warehouse manager".

1.title: Analyzing Requirements, continued
1.text: Analyzing Requirements, continued. Spot risks. "What could go wrong, and what would we see first?". Ask Claude to separate facts you gave from assumptions it made. Review and correct the assumptions. Requirements belong to the stakeholders, not to Claude. Claude drafts and challenges; people confirm. Measure success with numbers: "reduce average return processing from nine days to four". Exam tip: Analyzing requirements with Claude means clarifying, structuring and surfacing gaps, then validating with people. It does not mean Claude decides what the business needs.

1.title: Identifying Good Use Cases
1.text: Identifying Good Use Cases. Not every task suits Claude. Screen candidates on value, fit and risk.

1.title: Identifying Good Use Cases, continued
1.text: Identifying Good Use Cases, continued. The figure shows this: Screening use cases by value and risk: start with high-value, low-risk quick wins; plan carefully for high-value, high-risk; avoid low-value, high-risk.

1.title: Identifying Good Use Cases, continued
1.text: Identifying Good Use Cases, continued. Text-heavy work: drafting, summarizing, classifying, rewriting. Tasks needing exact, auditable calculation without verification. Repetitive tasks with a clear pattern. Decisions with legal, medical or financial consequences made by Claude alone. Tasks where a person reviews the result. Sensitive data that policy does not allow in the tool (Module thirteen). Work that is slow because of reading and writing. Tasks needing real-time systems or actions Claude is not connected to. Brainstorming and planning support. Tasks where an error would be unnoticed and costly.

1.title: Identifying Good Use Cases, continued
1.text: Identifying Good Use Cases, continued. Ask: How much time does it take now? How often? What is the cost of a mistake? Who reviews? Is the data allowed? Start with low-risk, high-value use cases, learn from them and expand. Keep a human in the loop wherever errors matter. Not every problem is an A I problem: sometimes a simpler fix (a template, a checklist) works better.

1.title: Research and Planning
1.text: Research and Planning. Research. Choose the tool by the question (Module six): web search for a quick fact, Research for a comprehensive cited report. For good results. State the question, scope, time frame and audience. Ask for sources and disagreements between sources. Separate findings from recommendations. Verify the key claims in the cited sources (Module four). Planning. Claude is a strong drafting partner for plans.

1.title: Research and Planning, continued
1.text: Research and Planning, continued. Scope and goals. Ask Claude for: Objectives, in-scope and out-of-scope. You check: Matches the sponsor's intent. Work breakdown. Ask Claude for: Phases, tasks, dependencies. You check: Nothing missing; realistic order. Timeline. Ask Claude for: Milestones with durations. You check: Durations against real capacity. Roles. Ask Claude for: A R A C I chart. You check: Real people and authority. Risks. Ask Claude for: Risks, likelihood, impact, mitigation. You check: Missed risks specific to your context. Communication. Ask Claude for: Update cadence and messages. You check: Fit with your organization. Claude does not know your team's capacity, politics or hidden constraints unless you tell it. Provide them, then review the plan. Ask for options with trade-offs, not only one plan.

1.title: Research and Planning, continued
1.text: Research and Planning, continued. Treat the output as a first draft that you refine with the team.

1.title: Process Optimization
1.text: Process Optimization. The figure shows this: Improving a process with Claude: map the current steps, find bottlenecks, redesign, pilot on a small scale, measure and repeat.

1.title: Process Optimization, continued
1.text: Process Optimization, continued. one. Map. How Claude helps: Turn a description or S O P into a step list or flow. Cedarbrook example: Returns: receive, inspect, decide, refund, restock. two. Find bottlenecks. How Claude helps: Spot waits, rework, hand-offs, manual copying. Cedarbrook example: Refund decisions wait for a manager's email. three. Redesign. How Claude helps: Propose changes: templates, checklists, automation of drafting, clearer rules. Cedarbrook example: A decision checklist plus reply templates. four. Pilot. How Claude helps: Draft a test plan and success measures. Cedarbrook example: One warehouse for two weeks. five. Measure. How Claude helps: Help analyze before or after data and write up results. Cedarbrook example: Days to refund, error rate, customer satisfaction.

1.title: Process Optimization, continued
1.text: Process Optimization, continued. Optimize a measurable process: choose K P I s before you start (time, cost, error rate, satisfaction). Claude can augment a step (draft the reply) or redesign the flow (remove an approval) (Module ten). Try changes small first (a pilot), keep humans in review, and expand only on evidence. Exam tip: Requirements are confirmed by stakeholders, not by Claude: the output is a draft with its assumptions listed for people to check. Exam tip: Start with use cases where value is high and risk is low, and keep a person in review wherever errors matter.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Requirements: Clarify, structure, find gaps, then validate with people. Facts versus assumptions: Ask Claude to separate them; correct the assumptions. Use-case screen: Value, fit, risk; start with low-risk, high-value. Strong fit: Text-heavy, repetitive, reviewed by a person. Weak fit: High-stakes alone, disallowed data, real-time systems, unnoticed costly errors. Research: Question, scope, sources; verify claims. Planning: Claude drafts; you add real capacity and constraints; ask for options. Process cycle: Map, find bottlenecks, redesign, pilot, measure. Measures: Choose K P I s before the change.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A manager says "Returns take too long." What is the best first use of Claude? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Clarifying and structuring the need comes first; people then validate it.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which task is the strongest candidate for Claude? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Text-heavy, repetitive work with human review is a strong fit.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A team wants to start using Claude. Which first use case is wisest? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Start with quick wins, learn, and expand carefully.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Claude proposes a project plan with a four-week timeline. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Claude lacks your team's real capacity and hidden constraints.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. For a comprehensive, cited competitor landscape, which approach fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Research gathers multi-source, cited findings; verify the claims you rely on.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two belong at the start of a process-improvement effort? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. Map the process and set the measures before changing anything.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Why ask Claude to separate your facts from its assumptions when drafting requirements? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Hidden assumptions are a main source of requirement errors.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. A team wants to test a redesigned returns checklist. What is a sensible next step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A small pilot with defined success measures shows whether the change works before the whole company depends on it.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Which factor makes a use case a poor fit for unsupervised Claude? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. High-cost, unnoticed errors need human review or a different approach.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Why provide your own constraints (budget, deadlines, policy) when asking for a plan? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Claude cannot know your budget, deadlines or policies unless you state them, and a plan that ignores them will not be realistic.

1.title: Practice Question 11
1.text: Question eleven. An operations lead wants to replace a manual approval step with Claude's decision on refunds of any size. What is the best response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Keep a human accountable where decisions have financial and customer impact.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: D. Question two: B. Question three: A. Question four: A. Question five: C. Question six: A and E. Question seven: B. Question eight: C. Question nine: B. Question ten: D. Question eleven: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
